chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, from al-Minqari, from Ali ibn Hashim ibn al-Barid, from his father, who said:

Ali ibn al-Husayn (peace be upon them both) said to me: 'Asceticism (al-zuhd) has ten parts. The highest degree of asceticism is the lowest degree of piety (al-wara'), and the highest degree of piety is the lowest degree of conviction (al-yaqin), and the highest degree of conviction is the lowest degree of satisfaction (al-rida).'

key_terms.الرِّضَا: Satisfaction or contentment with God's judgment
key_terms.الزُّهْدُ: Asceticism or renunciation of worldly desires
key_terms.الْوَرَعُ: Piety or God-consciousness, specifically avoiding doubtful matters

ai.seo_question: What is the relationship between asceticism, piety, and satisfaction in Shia spirituality?
ai.summary: Imam Ali ibn al-Husayn (AS) delineates a spiritual hierarchy where asceticism (zuhd) serves as the foundation for piety (wara'), which leads to certainty (yaqin), culminating in satisfaction (rida). This progression illustrates how detachment from worldly desires purifies the heart, enabling the believer to accept divine decree with inner peace, a concept central to Shia ethical theology. The hadith emphasizes that true satisfaction is not merely passive acceptance but the highest fruit of a life grounded in sincere devotion and certainty.
